premises.text: Mass retail cannot stock niche colors while prestige selection is expensive, so buyers face a selection-versus-price tradeoff driven by supply-chain volume constraints
premises.evidence_span: Walmart can't offer you all the colors that expensive prestige stores can, like Sephora

premises.text: Mink is a proprietary inkjet-like desktop printer that turns any image/hex color into FDA-compliant wearable cosmetics using commodity ink and substrates—no new software required
premises.evidence_span: Mink is a desktop printer that prints makeup

premises.text: Hardware retails around $300 with commodity-priced ink and substrates
premises.evidence_span: I'm going to retail this for about $300 initially

premises.text: Initial target is girls ages 13–21 who experiment with makeup online and have not formed brand habits
premises.evidence_span: My initial target market, they're girls, ages 13 to 21

value.text: Girls control the definition of beauty rather than corporations, by printing any color they choose
value.evidence_span: the definition of beauty is something that they should be able to control, not our corporations

secondary_value.text: Prestige-level color selection with mass/home convenience
secondary_value.evidence_span: It gives you the selection of prestige and it combines it with the convenience of mass

causal_links.evidence_span: they do this by charging a huge premium on one thing that technology provides for free
The Mink enables the web to become the biggest beauty store in the world
that's how we're going to change how the world buys makeup

notes: Mass vs Sephora selection/price folded as one color-access problem (§4.1.6). Inkjet workflow, hex picker, eyeshadow/lipstick roadmap, and FDA ink/substrates folded as one printer mechanism (§4.1.7). Speaker's stated priority (beauty control) used as primary value; selection+convenience as secondary_value. Founder bio and $55B market framing excluded. Anti-template: problem, hardware, and commercial/segment modules separately revisable.
